images.title: One square always left over
images.purpose: Show why a 5 × 7 grid cannot be tiled: tiles cover squares two at a time, so 35 squares always leave one uncovered.
images.composition: One grid centred in the frame, 5 rows and 7 columns, with a short label above, one caption line underneath and white space all round.
exact_structure: A grid of exactly 5 rows and 7 columns of equal unit squares (35 squares), with thin grey (#6B7280) grid lines; label above: 5 × 7 = 35.
Rows 1 to 4: each of the 7 columns holds 2 vertical tiles (one over rows 1 and 2, one over rows 3 and 4), 14 vertical tiles in all, filled teal (#0072B2) with thick dark outlines.
Row 5: 3 horizontal tiles over columns 1 and 2, 3 and 4, 5 and 6, filled amber (#E69F00) with thick dark outlines.
The square in row 5, column 7 is left uncovered, filled vermilion (#D55E00), with a small pointer label 1 left over.
In all exactly 17 tiles covering 34 squares, and exactly 1 uncovered square.
Below the grid, one caption line: 35 squares, 17 tiles cover 34.
rejection: a grid with other than 5 rows and 7 columns
more or fewer than 17 tiles, or more or fewer than 1 uncovered square
a tile covering 1 or 3 squares, or two tiles overlapping
images.takeaway: Tiles always cover an even number of squares, and 35 is odd, so a 5 × 7 grid can never be tiled.
images.description: A 5 by 7 grid covered by 17 coloured 2 × 1 tiles with one vermilion square left over in the bottom right corner.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video on why a 5 × 7 grid cannot be tiled.
images.teaching_notes: Ask students whether moving the tiles around could ever cover the last square, and connect the answer to 35 being odd.

image_decisions.why: Seeing one square always left over makes the odd count argument concrete.
